opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think it's a fair question, and I don't want to sound dismissive, because there will certainly be shifts. But a few things keep me from being too alarmed right now.

The first is that, if you actually look at how these systems get used day to day, they're still very much tools that augment people rather than replace them end to end. Take my own work in research: I use language models all the time for writing code, for brainstorming, for drafting. But someone still has to decide which problem is worth working on, judge whether a result is actually interesting or just an artifact, and take responsibility for what goes out the door. That kind of judgment, taste, and accountability is still really hard to hand over, and most jobs are bundles of many tasks, only some of which are automatable.

The second thing is reliability. There's a big gap between a system that does something impressive in a demo and one that does it robustly ninety-nine point nine percent of the time in a messy real-world setting with long horizons and lots of context. Agents still drift, they make compounding errors, they get stuck. Closing that last mile is often where most of the effort goes, and historically that's taken much longer than people expect.

Third, diffusion is slow. Even when a technology works, organizations need to restructure workflows, retrain people, deal with regulation, liability, integration with legacy systems. Electricity and computers took decades to show up in productivity statistics. I'd expect something similar here, which gives societies some time to adapt.

And finally, historically, automation has tended to create new kinds of work alongside destroying old ones. When something gets cheaper, like generating code, demand for it often expands rather than shrinks. So you might end up with more people building software, just in a different way.

Now, that's not to say I'm complacent. If we get much more reliable long-horizon agents, or systems that can genuinely do open-ended scientific discovery autonomously, which is something I work on, the picture could change quite quickly. So I think it's important to keep watching the actual empirical signals rather than the hype in either direction. But as of today, I see it more as a powerful amplifier for people than a wholesale replacement.

r001.rationale: The response cites human judgment, taste, and accountability as difficult to automate, but it does not say humans are the source of deep understanding.

r002.rationale: The response mentions brainstorming and changing kinds of work, but does not attribute limited concern to humans being the source of creativity.

r003.rationale: The response describes AI as augmenting people and concludes it is a powerful amplifier for people, connecting AI’s role to human capabilities.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that I'm not unworried, I just think the timescales people throw around are way too compressed, and that comes from spending a lot of time actually trying to get these systems to do useful work end to end.

When you look at a benchmark, you see a model that can solve a coding problem or write a research summary, and it's tempting to extrapolate from that to "this job is gone." But a job isn't a benchmark. A job is a bundle of tasks, and the ones the model nails tend to be the ones that were already the most legible, the most well-specified. The parts that are hard to automate are the parts that are hard to even write down. Figuring out what the problem actually is. Knowing which of the ten plausible directions is the one worth pursuing. Noticing that the thing you were asked for isn't the thing that's needed. That's most of what a senior person does, and we don't have great evidence that models do it reliably yet.

The other thing is that I've been working on systems where the AI is doing a lot of the research loop itself, generating hypotheses, running experiments, iterating. And what you learn doing that is how much of the value is in the scaffolding, the evaluation, the taste about what's worth trying. The model gets you volume. Volume is great, but it moves the bottleneck rather than removing it. Someone still has to decide what's good, and in my experience that someone is still a person for now.

And then historically, technology diffusion is just slow. Electricity took decades to reorganize factories because you had to redesign the whole floor around it, not just swap out the steam engine. I think we're in a similar spot. Organizations have to be rebuilt around these tools, and that's institutional work, not model capability work. So I'd say the risk is real but the clock runs slower than the demos suggest, and that gives us more room to adapt than the headlines imply.

r001.rationale: The response says people handle problem framing and choosing worthwhile directions, but does not attribute Lange’s limited concern to humans being the source of deep understanding.

r002.rationale: It discusses generating hypotheses and human taste, but does not attribute Lange’s limited concern to humans being the source of creativity.

r003.rationale: The response says AI provides volume while people evaluate the results; it does not characterize AI as amplifying latent human strengths.

astra-6.text:
I think the key distinction is between automating a task and replacing a job. A job usually involves a whole bundle of tasks, plus context, responsibility, and coordination with other people. Getting a model to do one part of that well doesn’t automatically mean you can hand over the entire role.

So I can imagine substantial productivity gains before we see widespread replacement. There’s also a gap between demonstrating a capability and integrating it reliably into an organization. That takes time.

That doesn’t mean there won’t be disruption, or that everyone will benefit equally. I’m uncertain about the pace. But I wouldn’t draw a straight line from impressive model performance to imminent mass unemployment.

r001.rationale: The candidate explains limited concern through the difference between automating tasks and replacing whole jobs, plus the time needed for reliable organizational integration. It does not say humans are the source of deep understanding.

r002.rationale: The candidate does not attribute limited concern to humans being the source of creativity.

r003.rationale: The candidate mentions productivity gains, but does not present AI as amplifying latent human strengths.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s a difference between automating a task and automating a job. A job usually involves a whole collection of things, including dealing with people, understanding context, and taking responsibility when something goes wrong. Making one part much faster doesn’t immediately remove the need for the person doing it.

There’s also a gap between showing that a model can do something and integrating it reliably into an organization. That takes time. So I expect substantial changes in what people do, but I’m less convinced that this translates immediately into mass unemployment.

That’s not to say it couldn’t happen. My uncertainty is quite large. But for now, I see a stronger case for these systems making people more productive than for them replacing whole jobs across the economy.

r002.rationale: The response does not attribute limited concern to human creativity or describe humans as its source.

r003.rationale: It says AI may make people more productive, but does not present it as amplifying latent human strengths.
